task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type X
AVOID labels based on opponent PPP
methodological_questions: Can opponent next-possession PPP be reliably linked to a specific offensive play type?
Are own-sequence lag effects substantial enough to bias play-type labeling?
What are the risks of lookahead bias when using future opponent possession to label current play?
What is the measurement reliability of derived play-type possession records?
Do sample sizes and exposure sparsity allow detection of meaningful differences in opponent next-possession PPP by play type?

historical_evidence.finding: PUTBACK is the top opponent play-type suppressor of star next-possession PPP for 6+ stars (e.g., D. Mitchell 1.178 to 0.884, d=-0.294, n_after=95; B. Beal d=-0.345 n=32; C. Holmgren d=-0.222 n=52). Other top suppressors: TRANSITION (A. Davis -0.058), POST_UP (N. Jokic -0.075). No multiplicity correction; n_after per play-type cell is 32-95 vs thousands of baseline possessions.

Q5c sequential triggering analysis found that rank-1 suppressor varies across players; e.g., Jokic after opp POST_UP 1.1271 (-0.0675, SE ±0.0500, n=480); Curry forced POST_UP -0.209. Rank-1 deltas mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; OTHER artifact flagged.

Play-type labeling audit found that 36% of OTHER possessions end in fouls, inflating PPP (FOUL_BUCKET); DRIVE PPP is 12pp below the foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK); PNR has 22% foul rate. Only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type.

PUTBACK suppresses next star possession via a fatigue mechanism: H2 delta -0.130 vs H1 -0.038 (22 stars); Q4 -0.289 vs Q1 -0.009 (11 stars, Q4 pooled n=34). After opp PUTBACK, offense PPP 1.097 vs 1.210 (d=-0.113, n=15,898). However, Q4 PUTBACK is sparse (34 pooled possessions at n>=30).

failed_approaches.what_failed: uncorrected exploration of opponent play‑type effects on star PPP
failed_approaches.why: No multiplicity correction; n_after per cell only 32–95, limiting generalisability.

failed_approaches.what_failed: formal testing of sequential suppression by opponent play type
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive because rank‑1 deltas were within 1–2 SE with no multiple‑comparison control and an OTHER artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: relying on derived play‑type possession labels for PPP analysis
failed_approaches.why: Labeling artifact: OTHER inflated by foul endings, DRIVE deflated; only 0.7% of possessions mapped via initiation_type, indicating pervasive misclassification.

evidence_establishes: Specific opponent play types (especially PUTBACK) can measurably suppress a star’s next-possession PPP, but effect sizes and significance vary across players and have not been corrected for multiplicity.

Derived play‑type possession records suffer from severe labeling artifacts (foul inflation in OTHER, foul leakage in DRIVE, extremely low mapping rate via initiation_type), undermining any analysis that uses those labels as a factual basis.
The PUTBACK‑suppression effect appears to be mediated by fatigue, with larger effects in second halves and fourth quarters, though sparse data limits reliability in late‑game situations.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the *offensive* team’s own play type (play X) affects the *opponent’s* next‑possession PPP, i.e., the exact direction and exposure of the research question.
Whether any opponent‑PPP difference is large enough to drive “AVOID” labels beyond what chance and data‑driven selection would produce.
That the labeling process itself, if informed by future opponent outcomes, is free of lookahead bias.
That sufficient sample exists for rare play types to detect a practically meaningful difference in opponent next‑possession PPP after correction for multiple testing and confounders.
own_inferences: Because the play‑type labeling is demonstrably unreliable (CHT‑025), any test of the hypothesis using the currently available derived records would likely be an artifact of label construction rather than a genuine basketball effect.

The direction of the effect (my play → opponent PPP) is distinct from the studied direction (opponent play → my star’s PPP); the former introduces additional confounding (e.g., opponent’s defensive reaction, transition opportunities) that the data may not disentangle.

Even if the labeling were perfect, exposure sparsity for many play types (e.g., POST_UP, PUTBACK) and the many‑hypothesis burden would make a well‑powered test extremely difficult without aggregation across seasons or teams.
uncertainties: What fraction of possessions can be assigned a reliable play‑type label using only the available per‑game play‑by‑play fields and the current graph‑database rules; a full audit of the label derivation is absent.

Whether the magnitude of opponent next‑possession PPP differences that would justify an AVOID label (e.g., 3, 5, or 10 points per 100) is realistically attainable given natural variability and court factors.
The exact sample sizes expected for each play type across 2022‑2026 data when requiring a clean subsequent opponent possession (no end‑of‑quarter, no substitution overlap complications).
The extent to which own‑sequence lag effects (e.g., how play X correlates with previous plays, score, and time) could confound the apparent opponent‑PPP difference without explicit control.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the retrieved evidence, the question would have appeared testable with a straightforward regression of opponent next‑possession PPP on offensive play type, perhaps flagged only for sample size. The labeling audit (CHT‑025) reveals that the derived play‑type records are likely unusable without major re‑engineering, and the two sequential suppression studies (APPA‑050, APPM‑022) show that even well‑defined opponent‑play effects are plagued by sparsity and multiplicity issues. Together, these findings shift the decision from a tentative ‘proceed with caution’ to a firm ‘do not proceed’ until labelling quality is demonstrated.

blocking_constraints.text: Derived play‑type labels are known to be severely flawed (only 0.7% mapped via initiation_type, foul inflation in OTHER, foul leakage in DRIVE), making it impossible to trust an exposure based on them.

Many play types occur infrequently; linking them to the immediately following opponent possession shrinks usable n, likely well below thresholds for stable PPP estimates after multiplicity correction.

If the proposed AVOID labels would be informed by the opponent’s actual next‑possession PPP, the analysis must guard against using that future outcome both as a label input and as a validation target.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work investigated sequential effects in the opposite causal direction (opponent play type → star PPP) and found suggestive but uncorrected results; a labelling audit exposed major flaws in the derived play‑type records. No prior study directly tests the effect of a team’s own play type on the opponent’s next‑possession PPP, nor whether such an effect is sufficient to drive AVOID labels.

risks.text: Play‑type labels are unreliable as shown by the foul‑leakage audit; using them as an exposure misclassifies many possessions, biasing any estimate of opponent next‑possession PPP.
For less common play types (PUTBACK, POST_UP, ISOLATION), the number of sequences ending in a clean opponent possession will be small, preventing precise estimation and inflating false positives.

Even with multiple seasons, total usable sequences per play type may be too low to detect a practically meaningful difference (e.g., 5 points per 100 possessions) with adequate power, especially after multiplicity adjustment.
If AVOID labels would be assigned based on opponent next‑possession PPP, the same future outcome cannot be used to validate the label without creating a circular, biased estimate.

Opponent’s next‑possession performance is influenced by many factors not recorded or controllable (opponent defensive scheme, fatigue from the preceding play, score/quarter situation, substitution patterns), and isolating the effect of play type X would require extensive and likely unavailable covariate data.

Testing many play types (possibly 10+ categories) increases the risk of finding spurious effects; any threshold for an AVOID label must be corrected for the number of comparisons, further reducing power.
If play types are retrospectively flagged as AVOID because of extreme opponent‑PPP values, regression to the mean will make future observed values less extreme, undermining the label’s validity.

The base rate of extremely high opponent PPP after any play type is low; a meaningful AVOID label would have to rise above this low background, requiring a very large effect that is unlikely for most play types.

design.estimand: The difference in opponent next‑possession points per 100 possessions (PPP) when the offensive team’s preceding possession is of play type X, compared to a baseline of all other possessions (or a reference play type), adjusted for game state, opponent strength, and fatigue indicators.
design.unit: A two‑possession sequence: your team’s offensive possession (coded with a play type) immediately followed by the opponent’s next possession (the first full possession after the change of possession, excluding cases where the quarter or game ends before the opponent’s possession completes).
design.sample: All such sequences from the 2022‑23 through 2025‑26 seasons (regular season and playoffs) for which a reliable play‑type label can be assigned using a validator‑audited deterministic mapping from play‑by‑play fields (not the current derived records). A staging audit would first be needed to demonstrate that > 80% of possessions receive a correct, unambiguous label.
design.power: A minimum detectable effect of 0.05 PPP (5 points per 100) with 80% power at a Bonferroni‑corrected α per play type would require approximately n = (2.8 / 0.05)^2 ≈ 3,136 sequences per play type, assuming an SD of 1.0 PPP; for 10 play types, on the order of 31,000 total sequences. Preliminary power simulations using historical possession‑chain counts would be mandatory.
design.controls: Inverse‑propensity weighting or regression adjustment for: opponent defensive rating (season‑to‑date or rolling), game score differential, quarter, seconds left on game clock, home/away, back‑to‑back indicator, and a fatigue proxy (e.g., player minutes played before the sequence).
design.falsification: Placebo test: compute opponent PPP after the *next* next possession (i.e., skip one opponent possession) and confirm that no systematic play‑type differences appear. Also, scramble play‑type labels randomly and verify that the observed differences disappear.
design.multiplicity: Holm‑Bonferroni correction across all defined play types tested. A global χ² test on a contingency table of play type × high‑PPP indicator (dichotomised above median) will be performed first to control family‑wise error.
design.decision_rule: A play type will be provisionally labelled AVOID if its adjusted opponent‑PPP is significantly higher than baseline (corrected p < 0.05) AND the effect size exceeds a practical threshold (e.g., ≥ 0.04 PPP) in both a training sample (2022‑23 to 2024‑25) and a hold‑out validation sample (2025‑26). No AVOID label will be finalised without replication in the hold‑out period.
design.data_version: NBA per‑game play‑by‑play files from 2022‑23 to 2025‑26 as of 2026‑06‑19, with possession boundaries and play type labels re‑derived using a publicly documented, audited mapping that addresses the OTHER/DRIVE foul artifacts reported in [prior work]‑CHT‑025. The re‑derivation must achieve ≥80% unambiguous labeling and must be frozen before any analysis.
